notes: Ruling slot 23 = House of Al Said under Said bin Taimur (MD icon kept). MD's second Al Said entry in 13 becomes the Muscat Interior Ministry of Sayyid Ahmad bin Ibrahim, so the dynasty is not duplicated. PFLOAG (the 1970 Dhofar front) goes to Communists slot 4 with starting popularity instead of MD's later PDFO in slot 3; its Maoist army is slot 19. Imamate-in-exile in 10, Oman Liberation Army in 7. Qaboos's coup circle in 0. Ba'ath kept in 21 per MD.

0.name: Halqat Qabus
0.text:
A discreet circle forming around Sayyid Qaboos bin Said, the Sultan's only son, who has lived under virtual house arrest in the Salalah palace since returning from Sandhurst and service with the British Army. Its links run through Tim Landon, Qaboos's Sandhurst contemporary now serving as an intelligence officer in Dhofar, and Buraik bin Hamud al-Ghafiri, son of the Wali of Dhofar.

The circle wants to replace the old Sultan's isolationist rule with a British-backed modernising monarchy: oil money spent on schools, hospitals and roads, an amnesty for rebels who lay down their arms, and a decisive military effort in Dhofar. Its leverage lies in quiet sympathy within the British establishment and among the Sultan's officers.

1.name: Ansar al-Sayyid Tariq
1.text:
The exile circle of Sayyid Tariq bin Taimur, half-brother of the Sultan, who broke with Said bin Taimur and left Oman in the early 1960s. Living chiefly in West Germany, Tariq keeps in touch with Omani merchants, exiles and British contacts, and is widely seen as the only member of the ruling family with the stature to head a government.

Tariq argues for a constitutional monarchy: a cabinet answerable for policy, a written constitution, eventually an elected council, and an end to the Sultan's bans on education, travel and imports. Firmly in the Western camp, he favours close ties with Britain, Iran and the conservative Arab states and appeals to the educated, the merchant class and Omanis abroad.

2.name: Al-Zinjibariyyun
2.text:
The Swahili-speaking Omanis of East Africa, uprooted by the Zanzibar Revolution of January 1964, which overthrew the Al Said sultanate of Zanzibar and killed or expelled thousands of Arabs. Scattered across Kenya, Cairo, the Gulf and Britain, and kept out of Muscat by Said bin Taimur's closed-door policy, they are the most educated Omanis anywhere.

Teachers, clerks, doctors and engineers schooled in English, they want a liberal, open Oman with passports, schools and a professional civil service that would let them come home. Pro-Western and anti-communist after their own experience of revolution, their leverage lies in the skills the Sultanate so badly lacks.

3.name: Ummal al-Khalij
3.text:
The tens of thousands of Omani men who have left home to work on the oilfields, docks and building sites of Kuwait, Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia and the Trucial States, since the Sultanate offers almost no wage work. In the labour camps and clubs of Kuwait and Dhahran they meet trade unionists, newspapers and radio, and their remittances keep villages from the Batinah to Sur alive.

They favour gradual social reform: paid jobs at home, schools, clinics, labour rights and a fair share of the new oil revenue on the Kuwaiti welfare model rather than through revolution. Pro-Western in practice, they distrust both the Sultan and the Marxist guerrillas; their weight lies in numbers and money sent home.

4.name: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-Arabi al-Muhtall
4.english: Popular Front for the Liberation of the Occupied Arabian Gulf
4.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Sha'biyya li-Tahrir al-Khalij al-Arabi al-Muhtall
4.text:
The revolutionary movement waging the Dhofar insurgency. It grew out of the Dhofar Liberation Front, which began armed struggle in 1965, and adopted its present name and a Marxist-Leninist programme at the Hamrin congress of September 1968. Led by a collective General Command, its fighters control most of the Dhofar jebel and took the coastal town of Rakhyut in August 1969.

The Front aims to overthrow the Sultan and every British-backed ruler of the Gulf, abolish tribalism, emancipate women and build a people's democracy. Supplied through Southern Yemen, armed and trained by China and courted by Moscow, it draws its strength from the mountain tribes of Dhofar and young radicals across the Gulf.
4.wiki: Popular Front for the Liberation of Oman

5.name: Al-Jabha al-Wataniyya al-Dimuqratiyya li-Tahrir Uman wa-l-Khalij
5.english: National Democratic Front for the Liberation of Oman and the Arab Gulf
5.native_full: Al-Jabha al-Wataniyya al-Dimuqratiyya li-Tahrir Uman wa-l-Khalij al-Arabi
5.text:
A clandestine guerrilla organisation founded in 1969 by former cadres of the Arab Nationalist Movement in northern Oman, to carry the armed struggle from Dhofar into the Sultanate's heartland. It recruits among students, workers returning from the Gulf states and dissidents in the towns of the interior and the Batinah, and is preparing cells and arms caches for attacks.

Marxist in outlook and close to the Dhofari revolutionaries, it seeks the overthrow of the Sultan, the expulsion of the British and a democratic republic for Oman and the whole Gulf. Its strength lies in secrecy, radical youth and links to Aden and the wider Gulf left; its weakness is thin roots outside the towns.

6.name: Ulama Nizwa
6.text:
The Ibadi scholars, qadis and mosque teachers of Nizwa, Rustaq and the inner valleys, the old seat of the Imamate that the Sultan's British-led troops occupied in 1955. Quiet under the Sultan's walis, many still regard an elected Imam as the only lawful ruler and Said bin Taimur's British-protected sultanate as a usurpation.

They defend sharia courts, Ibadi learning and the moral order of the interior against foreign influence, oil-company camps and Christian officers. Hostile to Britain and receptive to the anti-imperialist voices of Cairo and the Arab League that keep the Question of Oman before the United Nations, they carry moral authority over the tribes far beyond their numbers.

7.name: Jaysh Tahrir Uman
7.text:
The armed wing of the Imamate cause, raised in exile by Talib bin Ali al-Hinai, brother of Imam Ghalib, after the Jebel Akhdar war of 1957-1959. Trained and armed in Saudi Arabia, Iraq and Egypt, its fighters waged a campaign of mine-laying and raids in the early 1960s; today it survives as a diminished but organised body of exiles in Saudi Arabia and the Gulf.

It seeks to expel the British and restore the Imamate by force, cooperating opportunistically with Arab nationalist regimes and the anti-colonial bloc at the United Nations. Authoritarian and anti-Western, its leverage rests on Hinawi tribal loyalties and on veterans ready to return to the mountains.

8.name: Al-Lawatiya
8.text:
The Twelver Shia merchant community of Muttrah, living behind the walls of its own quarter, the Sur al-Lawatiya, on the harbour front. Of Sindhi origin and settled in Oman for generations, the Lawatiya are among the Sultanate's leading traders, with family firms in shipping, textiles and foodstuffs and close ties to Gujarat, Karachi and the Gulf ports.

Politically cautious and loyal to the throne that protects them, they follow the Najaf marja' Muhsin al-Hakim and seek communal autonomy, schooling for their children and freedom of trade. Their reformism is commercial and educational rather than revolutionary; their leverage lies in money, credit and their place in the Muscat economy.

9.name: Halqat al-Najaf
9.text:
A handful of young Omani Shia studying in the seminaries of Najaf, where the exiled Ayatollah Ruhollah Khomeini is lecturing this winter on Islamic government by the jurist, and where Muhammad Baqir al-Sadr's circle is forging a new Shia political activism. Returning students carry these ideas to the Lawatiya and Baharna of Muscat and Muttrah.

They reject the quietism of their elders, condemn both the Sultan's alliance with Britain and the godless Marxism of the Dhofar front, and dream of a political order guided by the clergy. Tiny and watched by the Sultan's police, their leverage lies in the prestige of Najaf learning among the community's youth.

10.name: Imamat Uman
10.text:
The Ibadi imamate of the interior, revived in 1913 and recognised by the Treaty of Seeb in 1920, whose last elected Imam, Ghalib bin Ali al-Hinai, was driven from Nizwa in 1955 and from the Jebel Akhdar in 1959. Imam Ghalib now heads a government in exile based in Saudi Arabia, with offices in Cairo and other Arab capitals.

The Imamate claims to be Oman's lawful state and denies the Sultan's authority over the interior, a cause taken up by the Arab League and by repeated United Nations resolutions on the Question of Oman. It stands for elective Islamic rule under Ibadi law; its leverage lies in Saudi patronage, tribal memory and international diplomacy.

11.name: Hizb al-Tahrir
11.text:
The Islamic Liberation Party founded in Jerusalem in 1953 by Taqiuddin al-Nabhani, banned across the Arab world and run from secret cells. Among Omani labourers and students in Kuwait and the Gulf states a few study circles have taken up its pamphlets, which travel home in the luggage of returning workers.

It rejects nation states, monarchies and Marxism alike as un-Islamic, and calls for a single restored caliphate to be won by persuading officers and notables to hand it power. Opposed to both superpowers and to British protection of the Gulf, it has no armed wing and no base inside Oman; its influence lies in disciplined ideological recruitment.

12.name: Jama'at al-Ikhwan al-Muslimin
12.text:
The Islamist movement founded in Egypt by Hassan al-Banna in 1928, which reaches Omanis through the teachers, preachers and students they meet in Kuwait, Qatar and Cairo, where Brotherhood members run schools and charities such as Kuwait's Social Reform Society. Its Omani sympathisers, mostly Sunni workers and students abroad, have no formal organisation at home.

It preaches Islamic renewal through education, charity and personal piety, demands schools and hospitals for a neglected country, and opposes both the Sultan's stagnation and the atheism of the Dhofari Marxists. Anti-communist and wary of the West, it relies on Gulf patrons and the mosque network.

13.name: Wizarat al-Dakhiliyya
13.text:
The Sultan's administration in Muscat, run by his Minister of the Interior, Sayyid Ahmad bin Ibrahim Al Said, while Said bin Taimur himself has not left Salalah since 1958. Through the walis and their small garrisons it handles tribal stipends, permits for travel and building, and the flow of information to the palace.

It stands for order, thrift and the preservation of the existing hierarchy, administering by letter and radio on behalf of a distant ruler rather than by any policy of its own. Neutral between the blocs and suspicious of all foreigners but the British, it is the only apparatus able to govern the country, and its officials are indispensable to whoever holds the throne.

14.name: Shuyukh al-Dakhiliyya
14.text:
The tamimas and shaikhs of the great tribal confederations of inner Oman, the Hinawi and Ghafiri factions that have balanced each other for two centuries. Many fought for the Imam in the 1950s and have since made their peace with the Sultan in return for stipends, recognition of their authority and freedom from interference in tribal affairs.

They stand for custom, Ibadi piety, the water rights of the aflaj and tribal autonomy, and distrust both centralising reform and revolutionary slogans. Outside the Cold War, their loyalty is negotiable: it follows subsidies, respect and the strength of whoever rules from Muscat, and no government can hold the interior without them.

15.name: Tujjar Matrah
15.text:
The great trading houses of Muscat and Muttrah, Arab, Lawati and Hindu Banian alike, such as Khimji Ramdas, established in Muscat since the 1870s, and the Zawawi family. They hold the import agencies, the shipping links to Bombay and Karachi and the credit on which the souk, the Sultan's treasury and much of the interior depend.

They want stability, British protection and the contracts that oil revenue, flowing since 1967, promises, but chafe at the Sultan's bans, licences and refusal to spend. Pragmatic and pro-Western, they finance whoever keeps the ports open; their leverage lies in money, import monopolies and the family ties that bind them to the palace.

16.name: Nawakhidha Sur
16.text:
The dhow owners, shipbuilders and sea captains of Sur, Oman's great sailing port, whose ocean-going vessels have carried dates, salt fish, timber and less legal cargoes between Arabia, India and East Africa for centuries. Their trade has declined since the loss of Zanzibar and the rise of steamships, and many crews now run cheap goods to and from Dubai.

They ask only for freedom: no import bans, no permits, low customs, open passage to the Gulf and the right to trade with anyone. Indifferent to ideology and to the blocs, they resent the Sultan's restrictions and the British patrols; their influence lies in money, mobility and the networks of the sea.

17.name: Ahl al-Aflaj
17.text:
The village communities of the date-growing oases, organised around the aflaj, the ancient water channels whose flow is divided by time shares and managed by elected agents and water councils. From the Batinah to the Sharqiya they watch the first diesel pumps lower the water table and threaten a system kept alive for over a thousand years.

They want the channels repaired and protected, limits on new wells, support for date and lime growers and respect for customary rules over land and grazing. Remote from both superpowers, their strength lies in the oasis farmers who make up much of the settled population and in the moral authority of village elders.

18.name: Jabhat Tahrir Dhufar
18.text:
The movement that launched the Dhofar revolt in June 1965, uniting Dhofari migrant workers, former soldiers and Arab nationalists against the Sultan. Since the Hamrin congress of 1968 turned the front into the Marxist PFLOAG, nationalist founders such as Yusuf bin Alawi bin Abdullah have broken away and keep the original programme alive among exiles in Cairo, Kuwait and the Gulf.

They seek a reformed Oman within the Arab nation, land, water and schools for the jebel tribes and the end of British control, but reject class war, atheism and the attack on tribe and faith. Their leverage lies in Cairo and Gulf patrons and in fighters disillusioned with the Marxist line.

19.name: Jaysh al-Tahrir al-Sha'bi
19.text:
The guerrilla army of the Dhofar revolution, some thousands of regulars and militiamen operating in units across the eastern, central and western jebel. Many of its commanders and political commissars were trained in China, and its camps teach Mao's writings, people's war and literacy alongside weapons drill.

Its radicals see the struggle in Chinese terms: protracted rural war, mass mobilisation of the mountain tribes, collective herds and the uprooting of sheikhs and superstition. Independent-minded and distrustful of Soviet caution, they rely on Chinese arms and instructors delivered through Hauf in Southern Yemen; their leverage lies in the guns that hold the jebel.

20.name: Qaba'il al-Jabal
20.text:
The cattle-herding Jebali tribes of Dhofar, the Qara, Shahra, Mahra and Bait Kathir, speaking their own South Arabian languages and long treated by the Salalah palace as subjects without rights. They gave the revolt its fighters, but many elders and tribesmen are alarmed by the Marxist assault on sheikhs, religion and tribal custom.

Their cause is Dhofar for the Dhofaris: an end to the Sultan's neglect and humiliations, wells, clinics and jobs for the jebel, respect for faith and tribe, and freedom from both Muscat's walis and Aden's commissars. Their leverage lies in rifles, intimate knowledge of the mountains and the ability to change sides.

21.name: Hizb al-Ba'th al-Arabi al-Ishtiraki
21.text:
The pan-Arab party of Michel Aflaq, whose Iraqi wing seized power in Baghdad in July 1968 and now seeks clients across the Gulf. A small number of Omani students and workers in Baghdad, Kuwait and Bahrain have been drawn into its clandestine cells, and Iraq offers scholarships, radio time and money to Gulf opposition groups.

It calls for unity, freedom and socialism: one Arab nation, the end of British protection and sultanic rule, and a disciplined vanguard state directed by the party. Hostile to Western influence and competing with the Dhofari Marxists for the Gulf left, it has almost no following inside Oman; its leverage lies in Iraqi money and patronage.

22.name: Quwwat al-Sultan al-Musallaha
22.text:
The Sultanate's army and small air force, commanded by seconded and contract British officers under Brigadier Corran Purdon, with Baluchi soldiers recruited in Gwadar and Makran serving alongside Omani tribesmen in the Muscat and Northern Frontier Regiments. Since 1965 most of its strength has been drawn into the war in Dhofar, where it holds Salalah and the coastal plain.

Professional, British-led and loyal to the throne, its officers increasingly doubt that the war can be won without money, civil development and a new policy in Muscat. It stands firmly with Britain against the Marxist guerrillas; its leverage is decisive, as it holds the only modern weapons in the country.

23.name: Al Bu Sa'id
23.text:
Oman's ruling dynasty since the 1740s, today represented by Sultan Said bin Taimur, who has reigned since 1932 and has governed from his palace in Salalah since 1958, issuing orders by radio and letter. He keeps the country closed: three primary schools, almost no hospitals or paved roads, strict limits on travel, imports and building, and oil revenue hoarded rather than spent.

The Sultan stands for absolute personal rule, frugality and the old treaty relationship with Britain, and treats the Dhofar rebellion as a matter for military repression. His power rests on British support, the army, tribal subsidies and the ruling family, but his isolation leaves even many of his own kin and officers impatient.
